source: Wang, Wang, Athiwaratkun, Zhang, Zou (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
finding: Layered ensemble where several different LLMs propose answers and an aggregator rewrites them. The paper says diversity of proposers matters and tests it with a single-proposer vs multiple-proposer ablation.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0: MoA 65.1% vs GPT-4 Omni 57.5%. Table 3, 2 layers, Qwen1.5-110B aggregator: n=6 multiple-proposer 61.3% vs single-proposer 56.7%; n=3 58.0 vs 56.1; n=2 58.8 vs 54.5; n=1 47.8 for both. Score rises with n.
quote: using multiple different LLMs consistently yielded better results
limits: Proposers were weaker or equal to the best single model in places; the same single model is not always the strongest (single-proposer used Qwen1.5-110B, not the best proposer WizardLM). Later work (c02) reverses the conclusion when the best model is used.
agent_relevance: Supports 'diverse attempts help' but the baseline was a weak single model. Our agent has one model, so only the single-proposer arm applies: +9 points from n=1 to n=6 samples.

source: Li et al (2025/2026 TMLR) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different Large Language Models Beneficial? (Self-MoA)
finding: Sampling six times from the single strongest model and aggregating (Self-MoA) beats mixing six different models. Mixing different LLMs often lowers average proposer quality. Over 200 experiments show MoA score depends more on quality than on diversity.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate: Self-MoA (WizardLM-2-8x22B x6) 65.7 vs 2-layer Mixed-MoA 59.1 (+6.6). Best single model WizardLM 53.1. Average +3.8 across MMLU-redux, CRUX, MATH. Linear fit of MoA score on quality and Vendi-diversity gives R2 about 0.7; quality coefficient exceeds diversity coefficient on all three sets, strongest on CRUX and MATH. Mixed task (Table 6): Self-MoA with best model per task 59.69 vs best mixed 60.04; TaskBest oracle 62.73.
quote: mixing different LLMs often lowers the average quality of the models
limits: Mixing wins when models have complementary strengths on a mixed task set (mixture of MMLU, CRUX, MATH): mixed 60.04 vs Self-MoA 59.69, so the difference is small. Judged by aggregator synthesis, not selection (see c04).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G4 and our single-model constraint: when quality is high, in-model diversity from repeated sampling beats cross-model diversity. Quality first, diversity second.

source: Hegazy (2024) Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning Capabilities in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks
finding: Debate between three different model families beats debate between three copies of the same model. Authors call it a Hong-Page style diversity effect.
numbers: GSM8K, 4 rounds: Gemini-Pro + Mixtral 8x7B + PaLM 2-M reach 91% (singles 78%, 70%, 64%). Three Gemini-Pro reach 82% with zero-shot CoT (80% without). ASDiv: diverse Gemini Flash, Mixtral, PaLM trio reach 94% (singles 89, 86, 81). Claimed to beat GPT-4 by 24% and Gemini Ultra by 14% on ASDiv/GSM benchmark comparisons.
quote: diverse set of medium-capacity models ... outperforms GPT-4 on the GSM-8K benchmark
limits: Small workshop-style paper, one run, no confidence intervals. The homogeneous baseline was run with the best model (78%), so the 78 to 91 jump may partly come from a weaker model correcting. Debate may be doing mostly voting (see c05).
agent_relevance: The strongest pro-diversity LLM number, but requires several model families; our agent cannot do that. Shows what a single model gives up: 82% vs 91%.

source: Maryanskyy, Budnikov, Kaliyev (2026) When Agents Disagree: The Selection Bottleneck in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
finding: Reconciles the conflict between MoA (diverse wins) and Self-MoA (homogeneous wins). Diversity only helps if the aggregation step can select the best candidate. Synthesis destroys the diversity signal; judge-based selection keeps it. Formal model: closed-form crossover threshold in selector quality.
numbers: 42 tasks, 7 categories, N=210. Win rate vs single Opus baseline: diverse (Opus+GPT-5.4+Gemini Pro) with judge panel 0.810; diverse mixed (Opus+Gemini Pro+Haiku) with judge 0.929; homogeneous 3x Opus with judge 0.512; diverse with majority vote 0.496; diverse with MoA synthesis 0.179 (preferred over baseline in 0 of 42 tasks). Glass delta 2.07. Decoupled independent judges: rank order kept (Spearman 0.90) but win rates drop 53-67% (0.810 to 0.611).
quote: selector quality may be a more impactful design lever than generator diversity
limits: Single round, one baseline, judge circularity inflates numbers; with independent judges the gain shrinks to 0.611. Exploratory weak-model finding not pre-registered. Open-ended tasks, not single-answer.
agent_relevance: Key for our agent: diversity of attempts is only worth anything if code or an independent check selects among them (G5). Synthesis by the same model throws the diversity away. Homogeneous team gives chance-level result (0.512).

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025 NeurIPS) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?
finding: Across seven benchmarks, majority voting alone gets most of the gain attributed to multi-agent debate. Debate is a martingale on belief, so it does not raise expected correctness. Also tested heterogeneous persona agents.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B average over 7 tasks: single agent 0.7205; decentralized MAD T=2 0.7377; sparse MAD 0.7330; centralized MAD 0.6551-0.6672; majority voting 0.7691. Arithmetic: single 0.814, MAD 0.43-0.84, voting 0.99. Qwen2.5-32B GSM8K: single 0.7566, debate 0.94, voting 0.9433. Persona agents (Table 4) GSM8K: single 0.8047, voting 0.9367; MMLU-ProMed single 0.7890, voting 0.8235; some persona MAD gains on ProMed.
quote: Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD
limits: Small models (7B, 8B, 32B) mostly. Persona heterogeneity gave a few larger MAD gains on Professional Medicine, so not zero. Theory holds for homogeneous, fully connected agents; heterogeneous case left open.
agent_relevance: Supports our rule: independent attempts plus a counted vote (code) beats free-form debate. Persona diversity added little over plain voting. Backs G4 and O-level sampling.

source: Jiang et al (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
finding: On 26K real open-ended queries (Infinity-Chat), 70+ models show two effects: one model repeats itself, and different models converge on the same answers. Ensembles of models may not give real diversity because of shared training priors.
numbers: 100 queries x 50 samples per model at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0: average pairwise sentence-embedding similarity within a model typically above 0.8; with min-p 0.1 temperature 2.0 still above 0.8; random cross-query pairs fall in 0.1-0.2. Cross-model average similarity 0.71 to 0.82 (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81). 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item; LLM judges and reward models miscalibrated on items where humans disagree.
quote: model ensembles may not yield true diversity when their constituents share overlapping alignment and training priors
limits: Open-ended chat prompts, not verifiable reasoning tasks. Embedding similarity measures wording and topic, not correctness. Causes not identified by the authors.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G4: same-model samples and even cross-model samples are highly correlated. Raw temperature does not make attempts diverse; diversity must come from structure (different framings, operators, constraints).

source: Vallecillos-Ruiz, Hort, Moonen (2025) Wisdom and Delusion of LLM Ensembles for Code Generation and Repair
finding: Ten coding LLMs from five families have complementary strengths (each solves some problems no other solves). Consensus selection falls into a popularity trap and amplifies common wrong answers. A diversity-based selection gets close to the ensemble ceiling.
numbers: Theoretical upper bound of a model ensemble up to +83% over the best single model (for example 112 to 205 solved on one benchmark). Diversity-based selection (CodeBLEU pairwise) realizes up to 95% of that potential, works with two-model ensembles; Defects4J ensemble 181 solvable. Naive consensus beat the best single model barely, and sometimes dropped (up to -15 problems on Defects4J, -6 HumanEval-Java). Benchmarks: HumanEval-Java, Defects4J, LiveCodeBench.
quote: consensus-based strategies for selecting solutions fall into a 'popularity trap'
limits: Needs several model families and a unit-test or similarity step; the ceiling is an oracle number, not achieved performance. Diversity-based selection still lost to naive in some two-model cases.
agent_relevance: Where attempts disagree, the minority answer is sometimes the right one. Majority-agreement rules (our G4 'hint, not proof') are backed. Use tests to select, not frequency.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Median of 12 different LLMs forecasting 31 binary questions matches a crowd of 925 human forecasters. Study 2: GPT-4 and Claude 2 improve when shown the human median.
numbers: Brier score: LLM crowd M=0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd M=0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850; no-information benchmark 0.25. Acquiescence bias: mean model forecast above 50% even though outcomes were nearly even. Study 2: Brier of GPT-4 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003) after seeing human median; accuracy gains 17-28%.
quote: This replicates the 'wisdom of the crowd' effect for LLMs
limits: Only 31 questions, one tournament, forecasts collected as three independent runs per model. Authors also note correlation among model judgments weakens the effect.
agent_relevance: Shows cross-model aggregation works for probabilities, but all models lean the same way (acquiescence). Same-model crowd would share that bias. Aggregate in code, with the median, not a self-judged mix.

source: Park, Schoenegger, Zhu (2024) Diminished Diversity-of-Thought in a Standard Large Language Model
finding: Tried to replicate 14 Many Labs 2 studies with GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) as simulated participants. Six could not be analyzed because the model gave the same answer every run (zero variance).
numbers: 14 studies attempted; 8 analyzable; 37.5% of original results and 37.5% of Many Labs 2 results replicated. Moral foundations survey: model said conservative 99.6% of the time and liberal 99.3% in reverse order condition, yet both showed right-leaning moral foundations.
quote: zero or near-zero variation in responses: with the supposedly 'correct answer'
limits: One old model (text-davinci-003); later models may differ (compare c06). Survey items about opinions, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: A single model cannot stand in for a population: persona prompts do not produce the variance a diverse human group has. Warns against persona voters (G4).

source: Chen, Saha, Bansal (2024 ACL) ReConcile: Round-Table Conference Improves Reasoning via Consensus among Diverse LLMs
finding: Round-table of three different model families (ChatGPT, Bard, Claude2) with confidence-weighted voting. Ablation removes multi-model diversity by using ChatGPT three times. A diversity metric shows cross-model answers are less similar.
numbers: Ablation on StrategyQA: using only ChatGPT as all agents loses 6.8 points vs the three-model team. Convincing-sample prompts add 4.5. Diversity (BERTScore similarity, lower is more diverse): three different models 0.8739 with accuracy 79.0%; three ChatGPT instances higher similarity and lower accuracy. Gains up to 11.4% over single-agent and debate baselines on seven benchmarks (e.g. date understanding 75.3 to 86.7; StrategyQA 71.3 to 79.0); with GPT-4 as a member beats GPT-4 on some. Random subsets of 100 samples.
quote: The effect of different models as agents is particularly significant
limits: 100-sample subsets, wide error bars; model-family gains confounded with having a stronger model (GPT-4, Claude2) in the mix.
agent_relevance: Same-model debate stalls (Degeneration-of-Thought, see c11). Confidence-weighted vote is code-based and could be kept even with one model, but cross-family gain is not reachable for us.

source: Liang et al (2024 EMNLP) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Names the Degeneration-of-Thought problem: once a model is confident, self-reflection stops producing new ideas. Two debaters with a judge, forced to 'tit for tat', break this.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic (GPT-3.5-Turbo): base 26.0%, CoT 28.0, Self-Consistency 29.5, Self-Reflect 27.5, MAD 37.0; GPT-4 alone 51.0. Common MT: GPT-3.5 MAD surpasses GPT-4 on that metric. Different debater models: Vicuna-13b 79.9, GPT-3.5-Turbo 80.4 (judge scores).
limits: Small test sets; forced disagreement prompt level is tuned and too much disagreement hurts. Later work (c05, c12) finds debate gains vanish once voting is matched.
agent_relevance: Agrees with our G1 (doubt on signal): a forced adversary can add one new idea, but it helps only on counter-intuitive items. It is a trigger-based operator, not a default.

source: Smit, Duckworth, Grinsztajn, Barrett, Pretorius (2024 ICML) Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
finding: Compared Multi-Persona, ChatEval, Society of Mind, Medprompt, Ensemble Refinement and self-consistency on medical and reasoning sets. Multi-Persona (angel and devil personas) was the weakest, and debate did not reliably beat simple prompt ensembles. Tuning how strongly agents agree changed accuracy.
numbers: On medical datasets every system beat single-agent except Multi-Persona; on non-medical sets single-agent beat all except Multi-Persona and Self-Consistency. First round to final answer: ChatEval modest gain, Society of Mind substantial gain, Multi-Persona decline. Agreement-intensity prompts tuned on MedQA improved Multi-Persona and other systems by several points.
quote: Multi-Persona ... leads to a decrease in performance
limits: Efficacy depends on hyperparameters such as agreement level, which authors tuned on held-out data; per-method figures are in plots.
agent_relevance: Persona-based opposition is the weakest form of diversity. Matches our rule of no persona voters on single-answer problems (G4).

source: Li et al (2024) More Agents Is All You Need (Agent Forest)
finding: Sampling many answers from the same model and majority voting improves accuracy with ensemble size; gains larger on harder tasks and weaker models. Small-model ensembles match bigger models.
numbers: GSM8K: Llama2-13B at ensemble size 15 reaches Llama2-70B accuracy; Llama2-70B and GPT-3.5-Turbo comparable at sizes 15 and 20. Scaled to ensemble size 40, averaged over 10 independent runs. Also a section on mixing GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in heterogeneous combinations.
quote: a brute-force ensemble of smaller LLMs can achieve comparable or superior performance to larger LLMs
limits: Gains saturate; benefit is largest where the answer space is small and correct answers are plurality. Same-model errors are correlated (c06, c07), so voting plateaus.
agent_relevance: Baseline for what in-model sampling diversity gives. Our approach should beat it only by making attempts structurally different.

source: Hu, Lau, Liu, Chen, Ng, Low (2025) DIPPER: Diversity in Prompts for Producing Large Language Model Ensembles in Reasoning Tasks
finding: Turns one model into an ensemble by feeding it an optimized set of different reasoning prompts in parallel. Prompt diversity beats sampling the same prompt. Optimizes a diversity-plus-fidelity objective (semantic volume).
numbers: Fixed ensemble of 7: seven distinct reasoning prompts 57.31% vs self-ensemble without prompt variation 55.76% vs average of seven single-prompt self-ensembles 56.55%. MATH with Qwen2-MATH-1.5B: ensemble n=9 gains about 10 percentage points (about 20% relative) over single LLM; three 1.5B instances slightly outperform Qwen2-MATH-7B; gain over self-consistency about the size of one model-size step. Spearman correlation of diversity objective with ensemble accuracy up to 0.8; U-shape trend over the fidelity-diversity trade-off hyperparameter.
quote: system prompts ... an influential yet overlooked source of diversity
limits: Small models, math sets (MATH 10% sample, GSM8K, MMLU-STEM); gain from prompt diversity alone is 1.5 to 1.6 points in the clean 7-prompt test; too much diversity hurts (U-shape).
agent_relevance: Closest published support for single-model diversity by instruction: framings and operator prompts, selected for fidelity as well as spread. Matches our O-operators idea; budget the spread.

source: Kim, Lai, Scherrer, Aguera y Arcas, Evans (2026) Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought
finding: Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B) show more internal perspective diversity (several simulated voices with different personality and expertise) than instruction-tuned models such as DeepSeek-V3. Steering a conversational feature raises accuracy.
numbers: Countdown task, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, SAE feature 30939 at layer 15: no steering 27.1%, +10 steering 54.8% (doubles), -10 steering 23.8%. Random conversational feature also helps but less than random non-conversational. Judge validation on Intelligence Squared Debates (N=1,196): LLM-judge counts voices with Spearman rho 0.86 (95% CI 0.84-0.87). Under RL rewarded only for accuracy, base models spontaneously develop self-questioning and perspective shifts.
quote: enhanced reasoning emerges not from extended computation alone, but from ... a society of thought
limits: Perspective counting uses an LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro), so partly circular; steering tested on one 8B model and one task; correlation within a trace is not independent attempts.
agent_relevance: A single model can host diversity inside one chain (internal voices) when trained to. For a scaffold, a prompt that forces a challenger voice is the cheap version; effect size unknown without training.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Multiple instances of the same chat model propose answers and then read each other's answers over rounds. Reported gains in arithmetic, GSM8K, chess move validity and factuality over a single answer and self-reflection.
numbers: Paper reports debate improves over single agent and reflection baselines on GSM8K, MMLU, biographies; more agents and rounds improve results with diminishing returns. Exact table values not extracted this session (opened for abstract and layout only).
limits: Same-model debate; Choi et al (c05) show a voting baseline recovers most of the gain. Source file was downloaded but table values were not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Origin of the same-model debate loop. Treat as an ensemble with communication; the communication part is the unproven bit.

source: Abdulaal et al (2025 ICLR) Balancing Act: Diversity and Consistency in Large Language Model Ensembles
finding: Neither maximizing consistency (self-consistency) nor maximizing diversity (MoA) is best everywhere. A consistency score gates when to use a mixture. Dynamic Mixture of Agents sets a new state of the art on Big Bench Hard mixed.
numbers: Abstract only read: no accuracy figures extracted. States that cross-validation bias helps when constituent models have the right expertise, and that arithmetic, commonsense and instruction following need different model capabilities.
quote: neither maximizing output consistency ... nor enhancing model diversity ... has proven universally optimal
limits: Abstract page only (mlanthology listing). Figures not verified.
agent_relevance: Argues for a code-computed agreement signal that decides whether to widen search. This is our G1 trigger (attempts disagree), supported in principle.

source: Thompson (2014) The Math Behind the Hong-Page Theorem (Notices of the AMS 61(9))
finding: Critique of Hong and Page (2004). The theorem is trivial once corrected, does not match the simulation, and the simulation shows the benefit of randomness not diversity. Replicates the simulation and tests maximally diverse groups.
numbers: Hong-Page simulation: n=2000 landscape points, l=20, k=3, 6,840 agents (20x19x18), compare ten random agents vs ten best. Thompson example: total pairwise diversity of ten random agents 131 vs 120 for ten best (45 pairs). Groups with maximal diversity performed worse than the median of 200 random groups of ten. Seven listed problems incl. Theorem 1 incorrect as stated, assumptions not met by experiment, best algorithm just checks every point.
limits: Critique of one paper; Page replied in his own writing that effect holds when agent pool is moderate. Thompson works on the n=2000 setup only.
agent_relevance: The famous result is about random sampling from a large pool of heuristics, not about 'diversity'. For a one-model agent: random differences in search may be as useful as designed differences, but the pool must be good (G4).

source: Romaniega (2025, v3) Fatal Errors and Misuse of Mathematics in the Hong-Page Theorem and Landemore's Epistemic Argument
finding: Re-examines the Hong-Page theorems, gives counterexamples when technical hypotheses are removed (e.g. injective V, unique best agent, clone performance), and proves a Hong-Page style theorem with the opposite conclusion, 'ability trumps diversity'.
numbers: No sample sizes: pure math. Contents list: sections on counterexamples for assumption 3 (V injective), assumption 8 (unique best agent), clone performance, a new 'ability trumps diversity' theorem, and an appendix proof.
quote: underscores the indispensable role of 'ability' in group problem-solving contexts
limits: Mathematics paper from econ.TH; not peer reviewed in this version; does not run agent simulations. Author says it does not deny that diversity matters.
agent_relevance: The theorem needs an agent pool where the best agent is not already near optimal and a good aggregator. Same conditions as c04. Do not cite Hong-Page as a license for persona diversity.

source: O'Brien, Fazelpour, Rubin, Wong (2025 CogSci) Epistemic Monocultures and the Effect of AI Personalization
finding: Agent-based model on an NK epistemic landscape (N=20, K=5) with agents that can query an AI oracle. A non-personalized AI makes agents converge and the community explores less; personalized AI preserves exploration if query rate stays low.
numbers: 1,000 simulations per parameter set; velocity (social learning) 25%; AI query probability 0.25 vs 0.75; half the agents with AI access in mixed communities. Non-personalized AI: random pick among the ten best agents; communities do worse as query rate rises, Hamming distance between agents falls fastest, and in the long run the non-personalized community converges to a suboptimal solution. At low query rates early rounds are on par with personalized. Personalized AI at 0.25 outperforms all other communities.
limits: AI is a modeled oracle, not an LLM. Standard NK parameters; results sensitive to rule changes (see c21). Numeric payoffs only read in text, figures not read.
agent_relevance: Models the exact risk of one model advising everyone: homogeneous suggestions cut exploration. For a single agent: the same applies to its own attempts if each reads the previous best (anchoring); keep attempts independent.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic Landscapes and the Division of Cognitive Labor (Philosophy of Science 76)
finding: Agent-based model on a hill-climbing landscape. Follower, maverick and control strategies. A mixed population in which mavericks (avoid already-explored points) stimulate followers outperforms all-follower populations; the claim is that cognitive division of labour helps. Only the search snippet was seen this session.
numbers: Not opened. The search snippet states the key result: in mixed populations mavericks stimulate followers to greater levels of epistemic production.
limits: Not opened; published replications (Alexander, Himmelreich, Thompson 2015; Thoma 2015) found the results change with rules such as the hill-climbing step and the landscape, and a 2018 re-implementation reported the code is correct but small rule changes alter the results (from search snippet, not opened).
agent_relevance: Maverick = an operator that avoids tried-before points. Our agent can do that in code by a tried-set. The result is fragile, so test on our own tasks.

source: Search snippet summary: replication of the Weisberg-Muldoon epistemic landscape model (2018 critical examination, reached via web search)
finding: A re-implementation in another programming language reproduced the Weisberg-Muldoon results. It also showed that small changes to the agent behavior rules lead to large changes in simulation results.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers read.
limits: Only the search snippet was available. Title and authors not verified.
agent_relevance: The maverick benefit is conditional on exact rules. Do not hard-wire a 'mavericks help' rule without a test.

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers (PNAS 101)
finding: Original simulation and theorem. The page could not be opened this session (PMC returned a browser check). Details taken from Thompson (c18): n=2000, l=20, k=3, 6,840 agents, ten random vs ten best; random group wins.
numbers: Group sizes ten; pool 6,840 agents (via c18, second-hand).
limits: Second-hand. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Reference point for the LLM translations in c03 and c04, which cite it explicitly.

source: Synthesis by this agent of c01-c15 (not an external source)
finding: Reading c01-c15 together: cross-family diversity helps when each model is of similar quality and when selection is by code, tests or independent judges. When one model is clearly best, resampling it wins. Synthesis by the same model erases diversity. Persona diversity gives small or negative effects.
numbers: Cross-model wins: c03 91 vs 82; c10 +6.8; c01 +4.6 at n=6. Single-model wins: c02 +6.6 (AlpacaEval) and +3.8 average; c04 homogeneous 0.512 vs diverse 0.810 with a judge but diverse+synthesis 0.179. Persona: c05 small, c12 negative for Multi-Persona.
limits: Synthesis, not a source. The studies differ in benchmark, aggregator and baseline, so numbers are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Rule for the scaffold: spend the sampling budget on diverse prompts and operators (c14), select by code or a held-out check (c04, c07), skip personas (c05, c09, c12), and keep one strong model rather than mixing in weaker ones (c02).

source: Wang et al (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Original method: sample many reasoning paths from the same prompt and take the majority answer. The standard single-model diversity baseline used by c13, c14 and c05.
numbers: Not opened this session. Cited as a baseline in c14, which reports DIPPER beating it by about the gain of one model size class.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Baseline arm for any diversity test in our harness (plain vs best-of-N vs scaffold).

source: Maryanskyy et al (2026) when evidence on correlated LLM errors: Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench tie-rate analysis inside c04
finding: LLM agents are not independent. Same-family model pairs tie more often than cross-family pairs, which is a sign of correlated outputs from shared training.
numbers: Chatbot Arena, 57,477 battles: tie rate same-family 34.9% vs cross-family 28.8%, chi-square 117.61, difference 6.1 points (95% CI 5.0-7.2). MT-Bench, 3,355 human judgments: same-tier 31.9% vs cross-tier 20.9%, chi-square 37.46, difference 11.0 points (CI 7.5-14.5).
limits: Tie rate is a coarse proxy for error correlation, and for human preference not correctness. Condorcet-jury reasoning in the paper also fails for open-ended text: majority vote gave 0.496.
agent_relevance: Numbers behind G4. The effective number of independent voters is less than the number of samples.

source: Maryanskyy et al (2026) weak-model and team-size findings inside c04
finding: Adding a weaker model to a strong diverse team with judge selection raised the win rate while cutting cost. With selector quality at zero, optimal team size is 1.
numbers: div mixed+judge (Opus + Gemini Pro + Haiku) win rate 0.929, original, 0.726 with two independent judges; div strong+judge 0.810 original, 0.611 decoupled. Exploratory weak-model effect p<1e-4, not pre-registered. Judge GPT-4o-mini was degenerate (ties on 99.6% of 1,260 comparisons) and dropped.
limits: Exploratory and not pre-registered; judge from the same model family as one agent; single baseline (Opus).
agent_relevance: Suggests a weaker, cheaper model in the pool does not hurt when selection is good; but conflicts with c02, which found low-quality proposers hurt synthesis.

source: Kim et al (2026) society-of-thought: RL and fine-tuning findings inside c15
finding: In RL on Countdown and a misinformation task, a base model rewarded only for accuracy grows more self-questioning and perspective shifts. Fine-tuning on conversation-style reasoning traces speeds early improvement over monologue-style traces and over the base model.
numbers: Early-training accuracy gains larger with conversational scaffolding than monologue in two tasks (figures not read in detail). Steering result from c15: 27.1% to 54.8%.
limits: Detailed per-step numbers not extracted; models are small open-source ones.
agent_relevance: Training-side evidence that internal multi-voice structure helps. Scaffold analogue is a challenger or verifier voice, triggered on conflict (G1).
